Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The umpires are back out in the middle and so are the players of New Zealand. The returning John Campbell will open the innings alongside Alick Athanaze for West Indies. Kyle Jamieson will get proceedings underway with the ball. Let's go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

The visitors will look to chase down 270 with confidence, whereas the Kiwis will be eager to utilize the new ball to get as many breakthroughs in the powerplay. The stage is set for an exciting second half of the contest! Stay tuned...

Windies' bowling was top-notch, with discipline and minimal extras conceded, but they missed a lot of chances. Shai Hope, behind the stumps, misses two clear stumpings and the fielding department as well dropped a couple of catches, which gave away the momentum back to the opposition. Jayden Seales bagged three scalps. Matthew Forde picked up a couple of wickets, while Greaves and Chase took one apiece, restricting NZ to a manageable total.

After being asked to bat first, New Zealand's innings got off to a rocky start, losing Will Young and Rachin Ravindra in the first 7 overs for just 24 runs. Devon Conway steadied the ship, falling just short of a run for his fifth half-century, before Daryl Mitchell took charge and anchored the inning exceptionally. He scored 119 off 118 deliveries and batted till the end overs to trigger the scoreline. The Kiwis' batting order showed depth, with contributions from the middle-order batter.

Windies have done a solid job restricting New Zealand to 269 at the halfway mark, setting up a thrilling chase. But we have to note that the pitch has given some assistance to the pacers, on top of that, the strong breeze helped the bowlers to swing the deliveries. The visitors will be feeling confident of getting a head start in the ODI series despite a late surge that saw the Kiwis score over 35 off the last 3 overs, giving them momentum heading into the break.

The call is for two and they get it as well. Full and nailed at the toes, Zakary Foulkes pushes the ball across gently through the mid-wicket region and scampers back for the second run. Jayden Seales closes out the innings well but New Zealand finish with 269/7 on the board.

She continues that 307 is the winning average here, but what makes this venue interesting is the dimension. It's 80 meters down the ground, 75 meters at the leg side of a right-hander, but 85 on the off side. ENds up saying that batters need to be tactful to scoop some boundaries.

Hello and a very warm welcome to all the cricket fans joining us for the build up of today's match! Tomorrow kicks off the first ODI of the three-match series between New Zealand and West Indies at Hagley Oval Stadium, Christchurch, and it promises to be a compelling contest. The Black Caps will be eager to assert dominance on home soil, while the Windies will be looking to upset their opposition with their firepower and strike bowlers.
... MATCHDAY ...

The T20Is are done and dusted with New Zealand taking the series, but not without the West Indies reminding everyone that Caribbean cricket still has enough fire to burn anyone on its day. Now, the all-format tour shifts gears into the longer white-ball lane. The ODIs. Some call it the ‘medieval format’ - not frenetic enough for the T20 generation, not purist enough for the Test traditionalists. Suspended in the middle, constantly fighting for relevance in a world obsessed with sixes, highlights, and instant gratification. But with the next ICC Cricket World Cup drifting closer on the horizon, this in-between format suddenly matters again. A lot. This series is a laboratory. Combinations to test, bench strength to assess, roles to define, and nerves to harden. Who handles pressure? Who carries momentum? Who emerges as a certainty and who slips into doubt? These answers won’t come from T20s. They come from ODIs. All of it begins at Ōtautahi - Christchurch - at the picturesque Hagley Oval, hosting its first ODI since 2022. And if you want a completed ODI? You have to go back to 2021. Yes, it’s been that long. Now, onto the home side. New Zealand may have just wrapped up a T20I series win, but ODI cricket is an entirely different creature. Fortunately for them, they’ve been a seriously consistent outfit in this very format. A Champions Trophy final berth, a 3-0 sweep of Pakistan at home, plus a tri-series win in Pakistan - the Kiwis have built a quiet, steady rhythm in ODIs. The challenge? Injuries. A lot of them. Big names are missing from both batting and bowling. And then there’s Kane Williamson, who’s retired from T20Is, skipping the ODIs, saving every ounce of focus for the Test series ahead. In his absence, the calm, calculating Mitchell Santner leads a unit that, on paper, still looks balanced enough to trouble any side. Expectations will inevitably fall on Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra - both elite, both classy, both a bit short on runs recently. Tom Latham isn’t in the best of touch either, with only 64 runs from his last five innings, which is uncharacteristically quiet for someone who is usually New Zealand's ODI metronome. A lot will rest on two of their most consistent performers with the bat - Mark Chapman and Daryl Mitchell. Chapman walks into this series in the kind of form that gives any dressing room a bit of comfort, with three fifty-plus knocks and a century in his last five innings. And alongside him is the ever-reliable Daryl Mitchell, New Zealand’s leading run-scorer in this format this calendar year, stacking up 642 runs with the sort of assurance that has become his trademark. Together, they form the backbone the hosts will lean on when things get tight. And bowling-wise, Matt Henry and Jacob Duffy have been their best bowlers this year, and lead the power-packed pace quintet, with Blair Tickner joining the squad after a very successful stint against England. Santner and Bracewell are the only reliable spin-bowling options who are well-equipped with batting skills, which provides enough depth in both departments. Across the field, ODI cricket has been the format where West Indies have struggled to find their footing in recent years. The talent is there, no one questions that, but consistency has been the missing ingredient. This will be their fifth ODI series of the year, and they have managed to win only one so far, against Pakistan, while their most recent assignment in the subcontinent ended in a stinging 2-1 loss to Bangladesh. They may not be stacking up wins yet, but there is a sense that West Indies are quietly piecing together a side that could find its footing sooner rather than later, provided they finally solve their jigsaw of combinations. Keacy Carty and skipper Shai Hope have been the pillars of their batting this year, both crossing the 500-run mark, but the drop-off after them is where the alarm bells ring. Whether it’s too much chopping and changing or simply a lack of consistent returns from the rest, the middle order has often been left exposed. That is why Alick Athanaze and Justin Greaves will be crucial in giving this line-up the stability it desperately needs. And when it comes to power-hitting, they do have the firepower. Sherfane Rutherford brings the flair, and Romario Shepherd can clear large distances without breaking a sweat. With only a couple of spin options, including Roston Chase, the weight of the bowling responsibility falls on the pace unit. Jayden Seales and Matthew Forde lead that group, while Shamar Springer and the young Johann Layne slot in as the supporting cast. It has been almost eight years since West Indies last played an ODI series in this part of the world, and since then, the entire core of their team has changed. Most of this squad hasn’t experienced these conditions. And if you look at history, the last time they won an ODI series in New Zealand’s backyard was all the way back in 1995. They did come close in 2013/14, managing a 2-2 draw, but a full series win has remained elusive for nearly three decades. While New Zealand hold a tremendous record at Hagley Oval, winning four out of the last five completed matches here. Can the Windies put on a serious challenge to Santner and Co.? Or will Hope’s West Indies rise up to their own hopes? A riveting series is on the cards.
